transcript.text: And at this point, for roll call and seating of alternates, I see Scott, Susan, Leanne, and myself. And so Susan's our alternate tonight. She will be seated to round out the commission to give us four. Oh and there's Ann Crummey. Okay so we've got now we do have an Ann, an Ann and a Leanne so that goes well. There we go.

The And so Anne Cremay is seated as well. The additions or changes to the agenda, The only change that I would see at this point is I would like to have Larsen spelled with an O instead of an E. Okay. Anybody else have any changes to the agenda? Okay, hearing none, that will be that. Next on the agenda is public comment. And I see we have, I think one member of the public joining us tonight, listed as Jan. I don't know that that is your name. Do you have any comments for the Planning and Zoning Commission at this point? No. Okay, very good. With that in mind, I'll go on to old business, which is advertised last time around, I wanted to spend the majority of the meeting on. One other person I see trying to sign in. Somebody just joined the conference and I don't know who you are.

Doesn't look like they have audio. Jed, this is Leanne. It might be me. I wouldn't take the password the first couple of times. I had to go out and come in again. Okay. I don't know that it's not someone other than me, but I had to do I

don't think it's you, Leanne, because it's been going okay since we got here. But anyhow, the other person that I had invited to sit in tonight was Hillary. And I forget her last name, but she's a limnologist. And she is working with the Alcoa and Alma folks. And I thought having her input as we went through the late Greg's presentation would be valuable. So she might pop in at some point here. I went through this presentation with the commission a couple months back. And since that time, I gave it to the Inland Wetlands Commission. And then I gave it to Alcoa and Alma at their meeting. And I thought we'd circle back here just because I don't know that it sunk in with everybody the first time that we went through it. But we had two people with us tonight who I'm hoping will

choose when we get to the next order of business to join us on the commission. We'll get there in a minute, but I thought it would be a good introduction to them and then get some feedback from you folks on the way ahead. I think we're sneaking up on a final product here and that would be that. So hopefully we'll get to the end of the Lake Reg's insured order. But the presentation that I go through with you tonight is what I would plan to do at the public hearing when we have that for the regulations. So with that in mind, I'm going to try sharing my screen here and calling that presentation up. And Mindy, I need your help to be able to share.
I just made you the cohost, so it should work.

Okay. And so this is the new and improved. Amanda helped us put a couple of pictures on the cover slide. So it's starting to look like something. And what I would like to do if people have comments as we're going through the presentation, talk about it here. What I'm hoping to do is get regulations that Jim can execute and execute faithfully according to the guidance we give him. And he needs to understand that we should understand what we're asking him to do. So the first slide here, proposed regulations and the goal, as we've said before, is to improve the quality of the water at Andover Lake. Some people would say, some people might ask, do we need this? And as we heard at the AlpoaAlma meeting, yes it is. Had, Hilary was one of the people who were doing lake sampling this summer and I think I said she's a limnologist who's out studying lakes and what makes those up and all those good things. I think she's working on her master's over at Yukon. And her master's project is going to

be on Andover Lake, I think. So that's why I think she would be a real good resource for her here. Oh, nice. But when she was out sampling, her report back to Alma was that she was shocked at the amount of weeds and algae growing in the lake this year. And so that's not what we're looking for. Nobody in the Lake District is looking for that. And so we do need to do something to go with that.
Does she have prior experience with the bleeds and the like?

I don't know if she had been doing that sampling. She gave a presentation to us a year or so ago and she's been working on it since then. So I do think she has some prior experience with us. But there was a lot of weeds in the lake nonetheless and it surprised her. So that wasn't the report we were looking to get. The other thing that we had talked about is that if the lake continues to slowly degrade in conditions, the Department of Energy and Environmental Protection could ask the town to put sewers in. That'd be very costly and not something that we're looking to do right this minute. So I think we all have an interest in getting the lake cleaner than it is that would be good. These regulations are modeled after the regulations that Columbia has in effect. And one of the things that we got from John Valeni and I did a spot check with a couple of people that live on Columbia Lake is that not only do the residents support the regulations, a lot of people, they do have they have taken ownership of the quality of the water in the lake, and they're out there doing above and beyond what the regulations require. And so that's a good thing too. And that's really what we're looking for. We would like the people around the lake to do the supplementary voluntary actions to get the lake better. And these regulations and the actions that we'd ask people to do will make the lake cleaner and healthier. And that's what we're all looking for.

How do we get contaminants into the lake? The rain comes down, it can pick up contaminants through the atmosphere as it's fallen to the earth, and it either goes into the lake or it goes onto the land and runs off into the lake, and that gives even more opportunity to pick up additional contaminants. The ones we're looking at most here are the phosphate and the nitrogen, which help the weeds grow. The other contributor to contaminants in the lake is from the septic systems. And most people that that I think might know something about the lake and contamination, they think that the septic systems are probably the major contributor to what's going on in the lake. I don't have any percentage what that is over the stormwater runoff, but septic is an item of concern. And certainly the Alma and Alcoa folks were most interested in what we were doing there. It's interesting, did review Columbia's regulations to see how they compared with what we were doing. And Columbia didn't tackle the septic system issue. I haven't seen John Felleny to ask why not. I don't know if that was a problem over there. They could be on sewers for all I know. I don't know.

The words we put in on septic systems are our own words in, so that's that. And so I'm thinking that maybe Kevin, you know, we'll talk about Kevin and Ann who are trying, we're looking to join our commission. Kevin's got a civil engineering degree and so maybe he can help me understand some of the stuff when we start talking about those septic tanks. Here's our map of the area again. The blue line outlines the Lake District. The red line outlines the watershed. And we're dividing dividing our watershed Lake District area up into four overlay zones.

The area right around the lake in yellow is what we'll call zone A. That's where we're looking to get a 10% reduction in contaminants going into the water after any improvements to the lot are made. The light blue is Zone B. There we'd be looking at a 7.5% reduction, a little further away, not as crucial that we make as much a reduction is we do with the Zone A folks. And when we get into the septic tank discussion, that will only impact Zone A and Zone B. The purple is zone C, that's the rest of the Lake District outside of zones A and B. And then the brown over in this area, that is outside of the Lake District, but still within the watershed area. So those are the four areas that we're looking at here. Last time we got together, you know, I was concerned about a spot like this here. It didn't look like it was much in

the watershed. Maybe it's got a little bit down here at the edge, but most of it's outside the watershed area. Would those guys feel that we were picking on them maybe? And the answer is that if somebody feels their property is outside the watershed, they can go talk to our zoning agent. Zoning agent concurs in that in the actions that we would expect if somebody in that zone would not need to be complied with. So that eliminated one of the concerns that I had last time we put this map up here. Any questions on? This is John Benda. I'm on the AMA board. Yep, John.
Linda Derek, our president, has no power so she cannot be present tonight. Hillary Kenyon had something come up so she won't be present. Okay. Thanks

for letting me know, John. That'll make the meeting shorter. I did have some comments from Hillary on the wording. We'll probably not go through that tonight. We'll save that for the next meeting, but we'll discuss that on the way ahead. So anyhow, now we'll start talking about the stormwater runoff mitigation. And one of the thoughts that we had was if you're making significant improvements to your property, we would ask that one of the improvements you make should be to improve the quality of the water running off your property into the lake so that we can all make the lake a little bit better. How much of what action needs to be taken will be determined by a nutrient allocation worksheet.

We'll talk about that in a minute. And as we've already said, for Zone A, we're looking at a 10% reduction. And that's a reduction of where you are before you start your improvement. So you take the lot where you are today. We would expect the final water to be built into the lake to be 10% cleaner than it is today before we actually start putting our building on there. We said zones B, seven and a half, zone C, five, and zone D, no worksheet would be required. And I hear I'm going it sounds like there's feedback on the line. Is that am I the only one hearing that or are you guys hearing that too? I heard it also, Judge. Yeah, I'm going to try and turn my volume down just a little bit, see if that I believe it was Leanne. I muted her. Okay.

Very good. I will put myself back up just a little bit then. So anyhow, that tells us what we're looking for is the final answer. We also say all zones must infiltrate the first two inches flush of storm water or volume. So if we get a two inch storm and you've increased the imperviousness, which means the quality of not allowing fluid to pass through it, soak into the ground, like you put, you know, one of the examples we're going to use is the partridges over on Lakeside Drive are going to put in a 400 square foot shed. We would expect that two inches off of the shed gets infiltrated into some mitigation measure going through that in addition to the 10% reduction. And then lastly, we can make minor improvements, which would be, you know, 100 square foot or less for Zone A, 200 for Zone B, and 300 for zone Z may not require a worksheet but still require the mitigation of a two inch rainfall runoff. So that's what we're looking for for stormwater runoff mitigation to help out the lake. I haven't shown you what a what the nutrient allocation worksheet is yet, but let's talk about when it's required. And if you're building a new building on the lot, you've to do a nutrient allocation worksheet. If you're improving more than 50% of the structure square footage within a ten year period, we're going to have a nutrient allocation worksheet for that too. We don't want somebody incrementally

improving their house and then all of a sudden they end up with a new house and they haven't done anything to improve the leaf. We're trying to avoid that. One of things that I had in mind for a question for myself is what does improve mean when you're improving the square footage? That could go almost to a total renovation to a coat of paint. And so Jim, he's the guy that has to do this. My thinking is that if you pull a building permit for an improvement, that's an improvement. If you're doing something like painting or putting up new paneling, new sheetrock maybe, but not changing any of the layout of the house that you don't need a permit, then that's not an improvement. So anyhow, that's still a little fuzzy in my mind but so be it. Increasing the floor area and again, it's Zone A, it's by more than 100 square feet, Zone B, 200, Zone C, 300. I think that's the one that's going to get most people anyhow, so I don't know this improvement of more than 50%, that's not redundant because we're going to get, know, all the action is going to come out of this increase in the floor area by more than 100 square feet. If you add an accessory structure addition, again the 100, 200, 300 square foot rule implies there that if you're putting up a shed, that would be an accessory structure that would you know,
get us into the nutrient allocation worksheet. That was

put in there, Jed, because if somebody does an incremental change over the years and doesn't fit into the square footage over a period of time, they would fit into the square footage. I gotcha. Yep. This catches it.

Sounds good, Scott. And I know we were talking at Elma and Alcoa about their similar words, but it talked about improving more than 50% with an increase in square footage for redoing the septic, were concerned about, okay, so you tear down a building, you don't make it any bigger, we still want you to comply with the improved septic requirements here. So thanks for sharing that with me, Scott. And then the last one on here is the increasing the impervious surface. And that would be, you know, somebody's putting a patio in their property, paving a driveway, something like that, we want to mitigate the runoff from that. So those are the conditions where we would get that nutrient allocation worksheet. Okay, so here's, now we get into the nutrient allocation worksheet and a lot of stuff here. What I want to focus on is in the Watershed District, we're going to put 151 Lakeside Drive, that's Partridges, they're putting up the 400 square foot shed.

That's in Zone A. There are lots 10,890 square feet for a quarter of an acre. So you plug in right now, I took these numbers off of Zillow, but they had a seven sixty eight square foot house. I looked at their driveway and said, yeah, that looks like about 600 square feet of gravel. And so I took the rest and put it in his lawn there, add those all up, and that comes out to their total lot size. And that gives us a total estimated load of 0.258 pounds of phosphate per year that they're putting into the lake. We said that for Zone A we want a 10% reduction, so we see that 10% of that number is 0.0258, and so that would give us the maximum load after proposed construction is 0.2322. So the first page is just telling us what the final answer is supposed to be. This is how clean we want the water after all improvements are made on the property. Any questions on that one?

Okay, we'll go down to the next one here. Now that we've got that, I've added 400 square feet to the roof because we've got 400 square foot shed there. I left the driveway the same and we reduced the amount of lawn by 400 square feet. So the footage is the same. Now we have an estimated load of 0.261 and the maximum load we're wanting to get is 0.2322. That tells us where we need to get down to. So that's all that this page is doing is this has given us the new load number that we're going to use on the next sheet to work our reduction on. Okay, so now we've gone into, and this is allowing us the different mitigation measures. And so if we're going from lawn to a mulch bed or lawn to garden, those kind of things, that will give us some reduction. What I'm most interested in is the paved surface. Step back. So in this case, to mitigate the increase, what we're going to do there is we're going to take

2,100 square feet of lawn and run it into a detention pond that will accept a half an inch rainfall event. And that gives us, you know, a minus 0.6 reduction in the phosphate load. That was the difference? Was took amount from a roof and you put it to lawn, well, let me go back up. Don't want to get myself confused on that. So we were roof 1.3. No, son of a gun. So I went through this thing and I thought I had myself all fixed up and now it doesn't work as good like I thought. I thought I could take this number, subtract the other one and get the number over there. But if I go In this case, it's not working. So I'm gonna have to go back and do a little homework on that before it makes sense. But that is what I thought was if you took your roof or lawn to retention pond or whatever, you take that difference and that's what it is. I don't see that one point zero point. So it should be 0.8 and here we're seeing 0.6. No, I don't have the answer for that one, Scott. I'll have to go out and take a look at it. But essentially, what we did on this is you know, if you put a number in the green area here, it updates automatically, it goes through the formula, it comes out with the answer for the reduction over on this side. This is a screenshot that I put into PowerPoint, so I can't redo that and get it to automatically update.

But we, by trial and error, came up with 2,100 square feet of lawn would give us the amount of reduction that we were looking for. So that would give us 0.2319. I think we were looking for 0.2322 or something like that. We've reduced it to more than we're required and we're good to go. So that gets you to the end of the worksheet. One of the things that I whoop, somebody have a question? This is Susan. I
have a question. What is the basis you used for coming up with the different factors Okay. For determining the nutrient load.

Yep. And so those factors, we came up with those because we plagiarized this worksheet from the town of Columbia. Columbia did have a little research going on over there. And so when we started off, know, let me go back. So one of the questions, you know, that we were working on, oh my, I'm all the way to the end. Let me get back. Something happened here. I went to the twilight zone. Here we go. Back to the Andover Lake, we say 0.32 pounds of phosphate per year per acre. That's based on a study that was done on Columbia Lake. I don't know if that's exactly pertinent to our lake or not. That's one of the things that I'm looking forward to getting Hillary's assessment on because she is much smarter on this than I am for sure and I would like to have some kind of knowledgeable scientific basis for the numbers that we're using. What With I

these factors here, they're just plagiarized right from the Columbia worksheet. I did go look in our regulation on stormwater runoff and we had one or two things in there. I think we had something at the high end, they were all about one, then we had one other area at the low end. And it might be possible that somebody just fudged in these numbers based on how bad they thought it was as far as allowing the water to soak into the ground or having it run off into the lake tried to make it look right. I don't know. But I do know that if you do these reductions, you will end up with significantly cleaner runoff water going into the lake, and that's the goal. So my thought was the science may not be exact, but the result will be what we're looking for. And I was pretty happy with that. No, no, I agree on that. I just was concerned,

especially when you go to present it to town meeting or any kind of meeting that there is a scientific or some sort of researched reason for using the numbers that you're using, not just that. Well, Susan, and that's why I've got to get,

I need to have somebody more scientifically knowledgeable on this than myself. I think I might have an in with somebody through Megan Lowley who's the wetlands chair. She's gonna try and get me hooked up with this fellow that's a UConn professor in his area of expertise is stormwater runoff.
And so I'm hoping to have this run by him before we go to public hearing. Okay. No, I just wanted to make sure that we were as sound as we could be before we go to public hearing.

Right. And if I'm only as sound as Columbia did the study, this was Columbia's, that's what we borrowed, I'm okay with that. I would like to have more and I would like to have somebody else at that public hearing standing there with me to defend it if need be. That's where we are today. Thank you.
Columbia ever get their allocation worksheet operating so that when you plug the numbers in it all works.

Not that I know of And again, one of the things when we were working with John Valeni, he was not all that fluent with the worksheet. And I thought he was the guy that designed the worksheet, but he did not. Somebody else was over there doing the worksheet, and then he would take the answer and he would go out in the field and he would make the mitigation measures so that we got the reduction we were looking for. So that's what I'll say about that. So what we did, and you probably don't remember, but there was on Columbia's worksheet, you would plug in this zone up here, LA in this case, and it was supposed to give you the 10% reduction, zone B would be 7.5 and that, so on. We couldn't figure out how to make that work and when I say we, that was Amanda worked with Jim and I one day

trying to figure out how to get this so that we can work it. And we couldn't make it work the way we were looking to. I'm sure that it can. But what Amanda did do for us was, so now we've got all three answers down here. So if it's in Zone A, we've got the answers, Zone B and Zone C, and we just have to pick the one that we're going for and subtract it off to get the final answer. So the worksheet could be better, but we have it so that it does work now. And Jim, who's the guy who's going to have to take it out in the field and come up with the answers, knows how to do that.
That's just the important thing. The worksheet is fine, but as long as we get the reduction

That's what it's all about. And again, one of the things that we all need to be doing when we're working this over, especially with the wetlands group, is if somebody's doing something that's going to have some excavation work in Zone A or Zone B, we should be encouraging them to put in some mitigation measures above and beyond what might be required by these. They've got, you know, 90% of the cost is getting the excavator down there to do the work and we'll go from there. So we should encourage those voluntary extra measures as well. But anyhow, we do have the worksheet so that it works for us. One of the things that, as we were going through this, the question came up, well, what is a rain garden? And so I just put a little picture in here of a rain garden. If you walk around the lake, might see one down across from where Kurt Dowling lives on the lakeside the Lake Road there. But it's just a little depression in the ground where the rain can collect. They put some plants in there and those plants are supposed to help absorb the water out of the ground so that it's dry and sucks up a lot of rain. But it's just a depression that you would put in there. So that's what a rain garden's all about. The one on Lake Road's very small. I don't know that it gets you a lot of mitigation effect, but at least it shows you what a rain garden looks like.
This one's going into Puget Sound, so Puget Sound.

Well, the next, you know, when we were talking, the last time that Jim and I got together and we were going through our numbers, you know, we were talking about what's a detention pond? And when we get to the sample calculations I have, when John, Jim and I were talking, we thought a detention pond was you excavate out a depression or a trench, can fill it full of rocks and that would be a detention pond and that sort of thing. When I look online, for examples, the detention pond can either be a dry detention pond or a wet detention pond, and it's just a rather significant sized depression that collects the rain when it goes into it. And your storm drains, your runoff can run down in here, it collects it, allows it to soak into the water. So that's when I look online to see what a detention pond is, that's what I came up with there. The next thing that we talked about and I'm really, this is my favorite now,

is a dry well. And so there's people that, you know, they take the runoff from the roofs, run it down through a gutter, run the gutters to a downspout and into a dry well. And there's a couple of different ways you can do that. But what a lot of people have are just these things. And I don't know if anybody knows what a Quonset hut is, but they are the old temporary buildings during World War II that are just kind of semicircular metal that you put two ends on and people lived in did all kinds of things there. Well, this looks like a little quonset hut that you put in the ground and you run your downspout into it and it's sitting on a bunch of crushed rock there, but it gives a spot for all the water to go and it slowly sinks into the ground.

And these can be covered up, grass grown over it, you don't even know that it's there. Another example of a dry well that I saw online looking, you would dig a big cylindrical hole into the ground and you would line it with the cinder blocks. Again, the storm water runs into the dry well, it soaks into the ground through the holes and all the cinder blocks and it disperses that way. And two things that all this rainwater mitigation does for us is not only does it keep the pollutants from going into the lake, it helps keep our water table healthy. So it goes down into the ground, the pollutants are attacked by the bacteria that are in the ground, so that gets rid of that. And the water sinks down into the water table and maintains a healthy environment for all our wells around the lake. So anyhow, those are examples of what we're looking at for these different mitigation areas here. Now we're gonna head back to the end of the worksheet

and what does the answer mean? And so we said what we were going to do is take 2,100 square feet of lawn and run it into, equivalent from a one half inch rain event into a detention pond. And so the first question we need to ask is how much is a onetwo inches of rain on 2,100 square feet of lawn? And so you multiply the 2,100 square feet times a half inch of rain with a conversion factor, one foot is 12 inches, and that comes up to 88 cubic feet of rainwater. That's what we've got to collect, that's what we've got to mitigate. Then we also said we were gonna take that two inches of runoff from the roof. So I took 400 square feet of roof times two inches of rain, again times the conversion factor to get it all into feet, and that comes out to 67 cubic feet of runoff water. Add these two things together, we're looking to mitigate 155 cubic feet of rainwater. So that's the amount that we've got to do something with. Now I got myself into the trench because I started working backwards from the line in our regulations that said if we were gonna do 100 square feet or less of added roofing or patio or whatever, we didn't need to do the worksheet. We could just dig a trench and fill it full of stone. So I said okay, and I asked what's a retention basin? And they said well that's

this, you just make it bigger. And I said, okay, well under the shed we will excavate down so that we can put a bunch of crushed stone in to get the volume to accommodate this 155 cubic feet of water that we're looking to store. If fill the excavated storage reservoir with crushed stone, we figure we reduce the volume by about half. So if we want to get 155 cubic feet of water, we need to have three ten cubic feet of storage reservoir filled with stone so that we can accommodate that. I looked at the stone pad area for the shed being about one foot larger than the roof, so it goes all the way around that we put the shed on. So I took 22 feet by 22 feet, and that comes out to four eighty four square feet area of the stone pad that we're going to put the shed on. Then I said, well, just to make the math easy, if we dig the storage reservoir nine inches deep, let's see what we get. So I took my four eighty four square feet times threefour foot because that put the nine inches to 12 inches conversion factor in there for me and it comes up with three sixty three cubic feet. Bigger than three ten, so we're happy. We're storing enough water underneath the shed. And so that's what Jim has to do when he's going out in the field to work with the guys to implement the improvements that we came up with by using the worksheet. There might be places if we didn't want to put all the water under the shed,

maybe there's places like on the side of your driveway. I've got on my driveway where water comes running down like crazy, runs down a hill and into the lake. Well, would be a good place to put a storage reservoir, dry well, something like that. So that's up to Jim working with the applicants to figure out where's the best place and the best method to mitigate the water runoff.
So the whole area under the shed is the reservoir.

Right. In this case, and I thought that would work. I know the last time we were going through this, there was some concern that it might rot out the timbers that you're sitting the shed on. And my thought was, well, we dig it. Stack the stone a couple of inch higher than the surrounding area so that the water would never get up that high, you can protect it. But again, a lot of different answers, this one seemed to work pretty good for this particular thing, especially when the applicant was looking at putting the crushed stone bed down to put the shed on anyhow. So that's how we use the worksheet to come up with the mitigation for the stormwater runoff. Any other questions on that process? Okay. There are a couple of special cases on this. And one of them is what if you can't meet the rules? Your lot is whatever size. It's so small and there's just nothing you can do down there. Now that I understand dry wells a little better, I'm not sure that that would ever be the case, but if somebody comes up with one,

the regulations give us the latitude that they can fill out a special permit, bring it to the Commission, that's the most cumbersome of all. But if somebody's saying, I can't comply with your regulations, they would come to us for what we could do to help them out on their behalf. Hopefully we won't get many of those. What if the land to be developed is not in the watershed? We talked about that earlier. They go to Jim. Jim agrees that, yep, I agree, it's not in the watershed. You don't have to do any of this stuff there even though you're on our map for being

in that area. One of the things that we started tackling before we held the Lake Regs in a bandage last time was there are a couple of lots around the lake that are wooded lots that haven't been developed at all yet. Since the wooded lot is the best lot there is, it's soaking up rainwater, minimizing that runoff into the lake, how are we ever gonna get 10% better than that? We can't. And so my thinking was, well, we talked about it. At that point, John came up and he was looking at, we will give them a credit of 2,000 square foot of roof, 3,000 square foot of paved surface, and 10,000 square foot of lawn. And my concern at the time was we've got all different sizes of lots. And so maybe if you've got a quarter acre lot or smaller, 2,000 square feet of roof, 3,000 square feet of driveway is a little much. I thought that was too generous in that behalf. Maybe that's good for the bigger one. So what I tried to do here was go through and I put if lot to be developed is less than a half acre in size, I used as an example 151 Lakeside Drive. And I said, Okay, we'll give them credit for seven fifty square feet of roof, 600 square feet of driveway, and 7,500 square feet of lawn. Anything above that, you have to go and mitigate. I just ratioed the numbers up by put one half acre to an acre, one to two acres, and greater than two acres. So my recommendation to the commission is that we use this sliding scale
